dataset.title: Garden Toolkit core plants
dataset.description: Curated starter dataset of common temperate garden plants with planting, timing, care and yield ranges.

sources.title: Garden Toolkit editorial seed data
sources.notes: Compiled by the Garden Toolkit maintainers from widely published, general horticultural guidance (seed-packet conventions, national gardening-organisation and university-extension style planting charts). Values are NOT verified field-by-field against a single citable source; ranges are intentionally broad and each record carries a confidence level. Treat as a starting point and verify locally.

transplanting.en: Harden off for 7–10 days. Plant deeply — stems root along buried parts. Outdoors only when nights stay above about 10 °C.

watering.en: Water deeply and evenly; irregular watering causes blossom-end rot and split fruit.

fertilizing.en: Rich soil at planting; potassium-rich liquid feed every 1–2 weeks once the first truss sets.

support.en: Cordon (indeterminate) types need a stake or string and regular removal of side shoots; bush types need little support.

pruning.en: Remove side shoots on cordon types; stop the main stem about a month before expected first frost.

pests.en: Aphids and whitefly, especially under cover.

diseases.en: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) outdoors in wet summers; grey mould in humid greenhouses — ventilate.

harvesting.en: Pick when fully coloured. Before frost, ripen remaining green fruit indoors.

assumptions.en: Typical home-garden range for healthy plants in a reasonable season; varies strongly with cultivar, climate and care. Greenhouse cordon plants are at the upper end.

directSowing.en: Plant (optionally pre-sprouted) seed tubers when the soil has warmed to about 8 °C.

watering.en: Most important from flowering onwards, when tubers swell.

fertilizing.en: Moderately heavy feeder; work in compost or balanced fertiliser before planting.

mulching.en: Earth up the rows 2–3 times as plants grow to protect from late frost and prevent green tubers.

pests.en: Wireworms and slugs in tubers; Colorado beetle in some regions.

diseases.en: Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) — plant resistant varieties, remove infected foliage. Common scab on dry, alkaline soils.

harvesting.en: New potatoes from flowering; main crop 2–3 weeks after the foliage dies back.

storage.en: Dry briefly, store dark, cool (4–6 °C) and frost-free.

assumptions.en: Typical home-garden range for healthy plants in a reasonable season; varies strongly with cultivar, climate and care. Early varieties lifted young yield less.

directSowing.en: Sow thinly in shallow drills in fine, stone-free soil; keep the seedbed moist until germination.

watering.en: Keep evenly moist; drought followed by heavy watering splits roots.

fertilizing.en: Light feeder — avoid fresh manure, which causes forked roots.

thinning.en: Thin in stages to the final spacing. Thin in the evening and remove thinnings to avoid attracting carrot fly.

pests.en: Carrot fly (Psila rosae): fine insect mesh from sowing is the most reliable protection.

harvesting.en: Lift as needed; main-crop roots tolerate light frost.

storage.en: Store unwashed in damp sand or in a refrigerator at 0–2 °C with high humidity.

mechanism.en: Both are hosts of late blight (Phytophthora infestans); growing them close together makes it easier for the disease to spread between them.
French marigold roots suppress some root-knot and lesion nematodes. The effect is documented mainly for dense marigold stands grown for a season before the crop, not for occasional interplanting.
Phacelia flowers feed hoverflies and parasitoid wasps whose larvae prey on aphids and caterpillars. Attraction of beneficial insects is well documented; the resulting reduction in crop pests varies.
Sweet alyssum strips supply nectar for hoverflies that prey on lettuce aphids; studied in field lettuce. Effect depends on distance and flowering time.
Often claimed that onion scent masks carrots from carrot fly and vice versa. Trials give mixed results; insect mesh is far more reliable.
Same scent-masking claim as carrot + onion; weak and inconsistent evidence.
Popular pairing; claims of improved flavour or pest repellence are not well supported. Both like the same warm conditions, which makes them practical neighbours.
Used as a trap crop for cabbage white butterflies and blackfly; may concentrate pests away from the crop, but can also build up pest numbers if not managed.
Traditional advice says onions and garlic stunt peas and beans. Little experimental support.
Fennel is traditionally said to inhibit most garden plants. Evidence is anecdotal.
Part of the "Three Sisters" (maize, climbing beans, squash) traditional intercropping system. Works best with climbing beans and in warm climates.
"Three Sisters" intercropping: squash leaves shade the soil and suppress weeds.
Borage attracts bees, which may help strawberry pollination; claims of improved flavour are unsupported.

reason.en: Limits potato cyst nematode and soil-borne diseases such as potato scab and verticillium.
